newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Pynzenyk says quit to save reforms.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Pynzenyk says quit to save reforms.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Monday accepted the resignation of his economics chief, Viktor Pynzenyk, who was so devoted to his job he kept a bed in his office but quit last Wednesday in a bid to save his country's reform programme.

"I wanted to show that we must not change course. It would have been worse if I had stayed in government while the process marked time or went backwards," Pynzenyk, deputy prime minister in charge of economic reform since 1994, told a news conference.
"I have become accustomed to working to the end, as long as it is possible to do something...but recently I have simply not seen this possibility," he said.
He was speaking after his spokeswoman announced that Kuchma had accepted his resignation -- at Pynzenyk's insistence.

Pynzenyk, 44, is seen with central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko as the guardian of reforms in Ukraine, where government and a conservative-dominated parliament have failed to pass a budget for this year and a stringent tax reform package he created.

Pynzenyk said he talked to Kuchma earlier on Monday and discussed the economy, which he said was at a turning point. "The president and I said goodbye to each other," he said with a smile when asked what they discussed.
But he said he had not met Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko at all since he put in his resignation last Wednesday, except during a visit by a Chinese delegation when their paths had crossed.

He made clear he felt parliament and government lacked the political will to push through the budget and tax reforms, without which Ukraine cannot receive a multi-billion dollar International Monetary Fund loan.
"I do not believe it is impossible to get the tax reform package and the budget based on it through parliament," he said.

Kuchma himself has repeatedly slammed the government and in particular Lazarenko who he says is to blame for the fact the budget is still not approved. "I am convinced that if the government paid attention to passing the budget then it would be passed," the president told reporters at the weekend.

Kuchma said the budget deficit would be six percent of gross domestic product, half of which was to be covered by foreign credits. "But there are none, and there won't be any until we pass the budget. Then what will we do, start up the printing presses again? Then the whole economy would collapse".
Pynzenyk declined to answer directly when asked if he would accept a new job in government, perhaps even as prime minister, saying: "I have never refused to work and I am ready to work".
He said tax reforms would bring the economy to life by inspiring domestic demand, adding: "But tax reforms in fact are blocked. Attempts are being made to emasculate them".
The reforms were first presented to parliament last November but parliament sent them back to the government and says it is still waiting for a new version to approve.

Pynzenyk took much of the credit for the successful introduction of the hryvnia currency last year, and his tough policies helped bring inflation down to 39.7 percent in 1995. Inflation is forecast at 25 percent this year.

Western diplomats were dismayed his resignation. But one Western analyst praised him on Monday, saying: "Thumbs up to Pynzenyk for showing some backbone. I think he was getting a bit tired of being the figleaf" concealing the reality of Ukraine's economy, which has been in decline in the five years since it won independence from Moscow.
